analysis.one_liner: Creates a voluntary public financing system for Senate campaigns funded by a surcharge on large federal contractors.
analysis.headline: The Fair Elections Now Act was introduced in 2014 with 19 Senate cosponsors and referred to the Finance Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let Senate candidates opt into a public financing program: in exchange for rejecting large contributions and relying only on small donations, candidates would receive lump-sum grants from a new Fair Elections Fund, a six-for-one match on small-dollar gifts, and vouchers for broadcast ads. The fund would be paid for largely by a 0.5% surcharge on payments under federal contracts worth more than $10 million. It also would have required broadcasters to give participating candidates discounted ad rates, barred them from preempting paid candidate ads, and let taxpayers claim a small refundable credit for Senate campaign contributions.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates who qualify by collecting a set number of small in-state contributions would get public grants, a 600% match on small-dollar donations, and broadcast advertising vouchers, allowing them to run competitive campaigns without large contributions [S3]. Ordinary voters would gain from reduced reliance on big-money donors, cheaper candidate ads, and mandatory candidate debates; a refundable tax credit up to $50 per person would subsidize small contributions [S3]. The bill's own findings argue this would reduce perceived conflicts of interest and make elections more competitive [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Participating candidates receive a base grant (at least $750,000 plus $150,000 per congressional district), a 600% match on qualifying small-dollar contributions capped at a multiple of the grant, and general-election advertising vouchers worth $100,000 per congressional district [S3].

To qualify, candidates must collect hundreds to thousands of contributions of $5-$150 from in-state residents and agree to accept no contributions beyond small-dollar gifts, public funds, and vouchers, effectively replacing large-donor financing [S3].

Broadcasters must sell participating candidates airtime at no more than 80% of the lowest unit charge, may not preempt paid candidate ads, and must report political ad purchases on a standardized form, lowering campaign costs and increasing transparency [S3].

The bill creates a refundable tax credit covering 50% of Senate campaign contributions up to $50 ($100 for joint returns), aimed at encouraging small contributions from taxpayers of all income levels [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies holding more than $10 million in federal contracts would pay a 0.5% tax on contract payments (capped at $500,000 per year), which the Senate declared should fund the program [S2]. Taxpayers generally would bear the cost of the public grants, voucher redemptions, and the refundable contribution tax credit [S2]. Broadcasters would lose revenue from discounted candidate rates and mandatory voucher acceptance [S3].

drawbacks.text: The program is voluntary, and the bill contains no mechanism to counter spending by nonparticipating candidates or by independent groups, so outside money could still dominate races involving opting-out candidates [S3].

The financing relies on a 0.5% tax on payments under federal contracts, a cost that contractors may pass through to the government in bids, and the refundable tax credit is a direct taxpayer expense [S3].

The bill's broadcast provisions impose new obligations on broadcasters, including discounted rates, a ban on preempting candidate ads, license-revocation exposure for denied access, and standardized political-ad reporting, which broadcasters would bear as compliance and revenue costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — publicly financed, small-donor-funded Senate campaigns, cheaper candidate advertising, and a small tax credit for grassroots contributions — come at a real but limited cost: a surcharge on large federal contractors and public spending on campaign grants and vouchers. The main design weakness is that the program is voluntary with no response mechanism to outside spending by nonparticipants, which limits how far it would actually reduce the influence of large contributions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee on February 12, 2014, and the committee never acted on it, so the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Durbin introduced S. 2023, the Fair Elections Now Act, in the Senate on February 12, 2014, with 16 original Democratic cosponsors listed at introduction [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced [S5].
Nineteen senators cosponsored the bill — 18 Democrats and 1 Independent; no Republican cosponsored it [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the February 12, 2014 referral, and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing private financing system remained in place: large federal contractors avoided the 0.5% contract surcharge, broadcasters kept current ad pricing practices, and candidates continued to rely on large contributions and high-dollar fundraising. Candidates dependent on big donors faced no new publicly funded competition.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big federal contractors, broadcasters, and large donors

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 2023 on February 12, 2014 and delivered introductory remarks; the bill was then referred to the Finance Committee, which he did not sit on

against.name: Chair Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 12, 2014; the committee took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote after its introduction

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the bill received no votes, so its fate divided along party lines in sponsorship if not in recorded votes.

industries.note: Companies with more than $10 million in federal contracts would pay a 0.5% tax on contract payments (capped at $500,000 per year) to fund public campaign financing [S3]. The bill died, so contractors kept that money.

Stations would have to sell participating candidates airtime at up to 20% below the lowest unit charge, accept advertising vouchers as payment, and file standardized political-ad reports, while also receiving voucher revenue [S3]. The bill never advanced, so current rates and disclosure rules stayed unchanged.

industries.industry: High-dollar donors and campaign fundraising industry
industries.note: Participating candidates could accept only small-dollar contributions, eliminating large checks to those campaigns and shrinking the role of bundlers and big-money fundraising committees [S3]. Nonparticipation remained an option, and the bill's failure left the large-donor system intact.
